dimensions.summary: The scraper has a sound skeleton — a stop-on-block kill-switch, a serial full-jitter cadence, and stable-hook selectors that demonstrably extracted 120 real amazon.eg products with 98-100% field fill and correct broad+leaf BSR. BUT it is not production-hardened. Two unhardened parse paths (rank int-cast on comma-thousands ranks; rating float-cast) will raise inside parse_bestsellers and cause an ENTIRE category to be silently dropped via run.py's generic except→continue. The kill-switch is marker-only with no positive page-identity assertion (canonical=amazon.eg / ue_mid / EGP), no soft-warning for CAPTCHA-at-200, and the only fill-rate guard (len<5) accepts degraded 5-14-row lists with no alarm — so a localized challenge or interstitial that renders ≥5 /dp/ links can be ingested as data. Writes are non-atomic and run.py destructively overwrites good real data with an empty file on an early block (trends.py has a keep-on-empty guard; run.py does not). The on-disk data is already provably stale/inconsistent: products.json review bodies still contain boilerplate that the CURRENT parse.py strips (older-code artifact), meta.json disagrees with bestsellers.json (books vs no-books; 135 vs 120 products), and keywords.json is empty so the app silently serves SEED keywords while advertising a real pipeline. Anti-ban cadence basics are correct but the spec's token-bucket, burst cap, daily budget, daily cookie-jar rotation, Retry-After honoring, and exponential cooldown are all absent. AR-session isolation is correctly implemented (verified good).

findings.area: Parsing robustness / silent data loss
findings.issue: Unhardened numeric casts raise ValueError that bubbles out of parse_bestsellers/parse_product and silently drops a whole category. Rank uses int(rank_el.get_text().lstrip('#')) with NO comma stripping, while the BSR path two lines apart DOES use .replace(',',''), proving this path was not hardened.
findings.evidence: Verified: int('#1,234'.lstrip('#')) -> ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '1,234'. Amazon Best Sellers badges show comma-thousands ranks (e.g. #1,234). Rating float('out of 5 stars'.split()[0]) -> ValueError. In run.py the call sits under `except Exception: continue` (lines 48-50), so the exception is swallowed and the entire category yields zero rows with only a generic [ERROR] log line.
findings.impact: A single product with a 4-digit rank or a non-standard a-icon-alt string wipes the whole category from that scrape. Combined with the destructive overwrite (below), a healthy category can vanish from the live UI with no alert.
findings.fix: Reuse the existing tolerant helpers: rank = _int(rank_el.get_text()) and rating via _num(...) (both already strip commas/non-digits and return None safely). Never raw int()/float() on scraped text. Additionally wrap each per-card extraction in try/except so one bad card cannot kill the whole list.

findings.area: Kill-switch completeness / challenge-page ingestion
findings.issue: The block detector is body-substring + status only. There is NO positive page-identity assertion (canonical=amazon.eg / ue_mid=ARBP9OOSHTCHU / EGP present) before a page is accepted, and NO soft-warning for the CAPTCHA-at-200 case the spec (§1.4) explicitly mandated (status 200 but 0 product nodes, or response-time spike). fetch.py never counts product nodes.
findings.evidence: fetch.py _is_blocked only checks status in {403,429,503} and 5 English substrings. The spec §1.4 required: 'Accept a page ONLY if status==200 and not blocked and >=20 product nodes parsed' and a soft-warning detector — neither exists. grep for ue_mid/ARBP9OOSHTCHU/canonical in scrapers/*.py: ABSENT in fetch.py and parse.py. A localized/Arabic challenge, a geo/continue-shopping interstitial, or a new markup variant that lacks these exact EN strings returns 200, passes _is_blocked, and if it renders >=5 /dp/ anchors is ingested as real data.
findings.impact: Garbage/challenge pages can be ingested as authoritative 'high confidence, isEstimated:false' amazon.eg facts and shown to users, defeating the entire stop-on-block guarantee. This is the exact silent-failure the spec called out as mandatory to prevent.
findings.fix: Before accepting any list/detail HTML, assert marketplace identity (body contains ue_mid=ARBP9OOSHTCHU OR canonical href contains amazon.eg) AND a minimum product-node count (>=20 for a bestsellers page per spec), else treat as soft-block (warn + skip, do not write). Add a response-time baseline warning. Extend markers with a title/<form action=validateCaptcha> check and Arabic challenge strings.

findings.area: Data durability / destructive non-atomic writes
findings.issue: run.py writes bestsellers/products/meta with plain Path.write_text (non-atomic) and ALWAYS writes even when the run produced zero rows (e.g. first category trips the kill-switch -> break -> all_rows=[] -> still overwrites bestsellers.json with all:[]). It has no keep-existing-on-empty guard, unlike trends.py which explicitly returns without writing when kws is empty.
findings.evidence: run.py main() unconditionally calls (OUT/'bestsellers.json').write_text(...) after the loop regardless of content; no os.replace/tempfile/fsync anywhere (grep: NONE FOUND). trends.py:96 'if not kws: print([SKIP] keeping existing); return' — proving the safe pattern was known but not applied to run.py. A reader (real-store.ts) or the concurrent scrape can also observe a half-written JSON because writes are not atomic.
findings.impact: A single blocked run replaces a full day of good real data with an empty file, silently flipping the whole app back to SEED data. A crash mid-write corrupts the JSON, and real-store.ts readJson() swallows the parse error and returns null -> seed fallback with no signal.
findings.fix: Write to a .tmp sibling then os.replace() (atomic) for all four files. Refuse to overwrite bestsellers/products with empty content: if all_rows is empty (or below a sanity floor), log and KEEP the previous file, mirroring trends.py's guard.

findings.area: Cross-file consistency / stale-artifact detection
findings.location: web/src/data/real/{meta,bestsellers,keywords,products}.json; written by run.py / trends.py with no version/schema stamp
findings.issue: The four data files are mutually inconsistent on disk and there is no schema version or content hash to detect staleness. The app trusts whatever is present.
findings.evidence: VERIFIED on disk: meta.json lists 9 categories incl. 'books' and product_count=135; bestsellers.json has 8 categories (no 'books') and all:120 — yet both carry scraped_at=2026-06-08T08:21:24, which is impossible from one main() run (now is computed once). products.json review bodies STILL contain 'Full content visible, double tap to read brief content.' even though running the CURRENT parse.py regex on that text strips it cleanly (confirmed: body.strip() != cleaned) — i.e. products.json was written by an OLDER parse.py. keywords.json is {keywords: []}, which trends.py's main() can never write (line 96 returns without writing when empty) — also a stale/foreign artifact.
findings.impact: Users can be shown a mix of data from different code versions and runs presented as one coherent 'as of 08:21' snapshot. meta.json (categories/product_count) is wrong relative to what the UI actually renders. Boilerplate leaks into displayed review text. Without a version stamp there is no way to catch this in CI or at read time.
findings.fix: Stamp every output with a schema_version and the git SHA of the scraper; write all artifacts in ONE atomic transaction within a single main() so scraped_at, categories, counts, and reviews are guaranteed coherent. At read time (real-store.ts) reject files whose schema_version != expected. Add a smoke check that meta.product_count == bestsellers.all.length.

findings.area: Keywords pipeline / silent fallback mislabeled as real
findings.issue: autocomplete() never checks HTTP status before r.json(); any 503/HTML/empty response throws and is swallowed by the bare except (line 78-79) as a per-prefix [WARN], losing that keyword silently. If ALL prefixes fail, kws={} and trends.py returns without writing — but the on-disk keywords.json is empty [], so real.keywords() returns null and the app silently serves SEED keywords while scrapedAt()/meta advertise a fresh real pipeline.
findings.evidence: trends.py autocomplete: r = creq.get(...); data = r.json() with no r.status_code / raise_for_status check (grep confirms no status handling in trends.py). real-store.ts:223 'if (!kw.length) return null'; data.ts:285-286 'const realKw = real.keywords(opts); if (realKw) return realKw;' then falls through to KEYWORDS seed synthesis. keywords.json on disk = {keywords: []}. The Demand Radar screen therefore shows synthetic keywords with no visible distinction from the rest of the 'real' UI.
findings.impact: The 'Demand Radar' feature presents fabricated seed keywords as part of a platform branded as running on REAL amazon.eg data — a correctness/trust violation. Block or markup change on completion.amazon.co.uk degrades to fake data with zero operator signal.
findings.fix: In autocomplete(), check r.status_code==200 and content-type JSON before .json(); on block, raise to trip a stop-on-block like run.py. Distinguish 'no real keywords available' from 'real keywords empty' so the UI can hide the section or badge it, rather than silently swapping in seed data. Never let an empty keywords.json coexist with a fresh scraped_at.

findings.area: Fill-rate health monitor (spec §2.0) missing
findings.location: scrapers/run.py:52 (only guard); no telemetry/scrape_runs record anywhere
findings.issue: The spec mandated a fill-rate health monitor (alert if title fill-rate < 90% or ASIN count < 5) and a scrape_runs record. The only implemented check is len(rows) < 5 -> skip. Lists of 5-14 rows (a healthy page has 30) are accepted silently, no title-fill-rate is computed, and meta.json records only SUCCEEDED categories — failures and partials are invisible.
findings.evidence: run.py:52 'if len(rows) < 5: [WARN] skipping'. No code computes title/price fill-rate as a health signal; grep for fill.rate/health/alarm/scrape_run in scrapers/*.py finds only the comment on line 52 and the unrelated 'health' category. meta.json is built from bestsellers.keys() (successes only); there is no errors[] or per-category expected-vs-got.
findings.impact: Amazon markup drift that halves the parsed rows, or a partial render, ingests degraded data and shrinks the leaderboards with no operator alarm. Silent quality erosion — the exact failure mode the spec's health monitor was meant to catch.
findings.fix: Compute and log per-page fill-rate (parsed/expected, title-fill %, price-fill %); treat <90% title-fill or <20 nodes on a bestsellers page as a soft failure that warns and does NOT overwrite. Emit a scrape_runs/meta.errors record listing every category attempted with status (ok/partial/blocked/failed) so partials are observable.

findings.area: Kill-switch scope on secondary fetches
findings.location: scrapers/run.py:58-64 (AR pass) and the autocomplete loop in trends.py:74-92
findings.issue: A Blocked on the Arabic title pass is caught by a generic `except Exception` and only logged as [WARN] — the run CONTINUES hammering subsequent categories after Amazon has started challenging. Only the EN bestsellers and EN detail fetches honor stop-on-block via the dedicated except fetch.Blocked branch.
findings.evidence: run.py:59 ar_html = fetch.fetch(...lang='ar') is inside `try/except Exception as e: [WARN]` (lines 58-64). fetch.Blocked is a subclass of Exception, so an AR-side block does NOT break the run — it proceeds to the next category and keeps requesting. The EN paths (lines 45-47, 83-85) correctly break. Asymmetric kill-switch.
findings.impact: Once amazon.eg begins blocking, the AR pass swallows the signal and the scraper keeps issuing requests, raising abuse score on the user's home IP instead of stopping — undermining the stop-on-block safety the project leans on.
findings.fix: Catch fetch.Blocked explicitly in the AR pass and re-raise / break the outer loop (or set a global stop flag) exactly like the EN paths, so ANY block anywhere halts the cycle.

findings.area: Anti-ban cadence vs spec
findings.issue: Core cadence is correct (serial, single connection, full-jitter 10-18s, never <8s) but several spec-mandated anti-ban controls are absent: token bucket (capacity 3, 1/12s), burst cap (<=20/10min), daily budget (150-200), daily cookie-jar rotation, Retry-After honoring, and exponential cooldown/strikes (30m/2h/6h/24h). The launchd schedule is fixed :07/:13 rather than per-run randomized minute offsets.
findings.evidence: _throttle implements only a per-request uniform(10,18) sleep. grep for token/bucket/refill, retry-after, strike/cooldown/2**, rotate/session-id: all ABSENT. _JAR is a module global never reset per day (only saved because the process exits each cron run). plist Minute=7 and Minute=13 are static.
findings.impact: On a single residential home IP the missing burst/daily caps and stale-session (no daily rotation) raise long-run ban risk; lack of Retry-After/cooldown means after a manual re-run the scraper could re-hit during Amazon's cooldown window. Lower severity because the per-request jitter + serial + small daily volume (~30-40 fetches) already keeps cadence conservative.
findings.fix: Add a token-bucket limiter and a hard daily fetch counter that aborts when exceeded; rotate the cookie jar (new session-id) once per day; honor Retry-After and apply the spec's exponential cooldown on a hard trip; randomize the launchd minute offset per install or add in-script startup jitter.

findings.area: Parsing edge cases (NBSP, out-of-stock, dedupe) — mostly correct
findings.issue: Most edge cases are handled well and verified, with two minor residuals: (a) currency is hard-coded 'EGP' with no validation against the page (acceptable given forced locale, but not asserted); (b) review body can be '' (empty string) which is stored as-is and later surfaces as an empty review card.
findings.evidence: VERIFIED GOOD: _num strips \xa0 NBSP (line 19); dedupe via seen set produced 120 unique/120 asins on real data; out-of-stock price stored as null and row kept (117/120 priced, 3 nulls present and retained); BSR captured both broad+leaf correctly (e.g. B0CPC8JMCW -> Electronics #1 + USB Cables #1). Residual: parse.py:136 body defaults to '' and is stored without a non-empty guard; currency literal 'EGP' at lines 75,169.
findings.impact: Minor: an empty-body review renders as a blank quote; a future non-EGP locale slip would be mislabeled EGP. No data-integrity threat today.
findings.fix: Drop reviews whose cleaned body AND title are both empty; derive currency from the page price string (it already prefixes 'EGP') or assert it, rather than hard-coding.

findings.area: Trends fallback / pytrends monkeypatch fragility
findings.issue: The Google Trends enhancement monkeypatches urllib3 Retry.__init__ at runtime and swallows all errors. It is best-effort and correctly skips on failure, but the noise filter the spec required (drop rising rows lacking the seed token / brand whitelist) is only partially present — it keeps a rising query only if it already exists as an autocomplete key, which is reasonable but means most Trends 'rising' signal is discarded silently.
findings.evidence: trends.py:65 'if q in kws: kws[q]['trend']='rising'' — a Trends rising term that is not already an autocomplete suggestion is dropped. The monkeypatch (lines 47-53) mutates a third-party class globally. Whole function is under one try/except (line 68) printing [SKIP] on any error. Given keywords.json is empty anyway, this path currently contributes nothing.
findings.impact: Low: Trends enrichment is honestly optional and labeled; worst case it adds zero rising tags. The global monkeypatch could theoretically affect other urllib3 users in the same process, but the process is single-purpose.
findings.fix: Scope the Retry patch with try/finally to restore the original, or pin a pytrends/urllib3 combo that doesn't need it. Reconsider whether Trends rising terms not in the autocomplete set should still surface (with provenance) rather than being dropped.

verified: Kill-switch raises Blocked on HTTP 403/429/503 and on 5 English challenge body-markers (fetch.py:50-54); EN bestsellers loop (run.py:45-47) and EN detail loop (run.py:83-85) both `break` on Blocked — stop-on-block works for the primary fetch paths.
Anti-ban cadence core is correct: serial single-connection requests, full-jitter delay random.uniform(10,18)s enforced between requests, documented never <8s (fetch.py:57-63).

AR-session isolation is correctly implemented and NOT polluting EN: response cookies are persisted into _JAR only when lang=='en' (fetch.py:78), and the AR request uses a local {**_JAR, lc-acbeg:ar_AE} snapshot so Arabic Set-Cookie never mutates the canonical English session.
NBSP handling is correct: _num replaces \xa0 before the numeric regex (parse.py:19); verified prices parsed cleanly from 'EGP\xa049.99'-style strings.
Out-of-stock handling is correct: missing price element -> price=None and the row is KEPT (parse.py:52-53); verified on real data (117/120 priced, 3 nulls retained, 120 rows total).
Dedupe is correct: `seen` set keyed on ASIN prevents the ~3x card re-renders from duplicating; verified 120 unique ASINs / 120 rows on live data.

BSR extraction works and is a genuine (non-artifact) parse: captures both broad and leaf ranks from the .eg table via the 'Best Sellers Rank' text anchor (parse.py:118-127); verified B0CPC8JMCW -> Electronics #1 + USB Cables #1, B098TYYKV6 -> Fashion #1 + Men's Boxer Shorts #1.

Selectors use stable hooks, not hashed classes: id^=p13n-asin-index / #gridItemRoot, span.zg-bdg-text, p13n-sc-* substring, data-hook camelCase values, /dp/([A-Z0-9]{10}) regex (parse.py:34-67,130-146) — matches the spec's stability rule.
trends.py has a correct keep-existing-on-empty guard: if kws is empty it returns WITHOUT writing keywords.json (trends.py:96-98), preventing destruction of prior good keyword data.
Bestsellers list fill rates on the current real file are healthy: title 100%, rating 100%, reviews 100%, rank 100%, price 98%, title_ar 100%, image_url 100% (120 rows).
notVerified: Whether the kill-switch trips correctly against a LIVE amazon.eg block (503/CAPTCHA) — not exercised; the instruction forbids fetching amazon.eg, so block behavior is verified only by code reading, not runtime.

Whether completion.amazon.co.uk autocomplete currently returns real EG suggestions — keywords.json on disk is empty and trends.py was not run; the live endpoint behavior is unverified (could be blocked, changed, or rate-limited).
Whether the pytrends monkeypatch + TrendReq path actually succeeds against Google Trends today — the [SKIP] path swallows failures and no run output was available to confirm.

Whether parse_product BSR/reviews selectors still match the CURRENT live .eg markup — validated only against the on-disk products.json, which is provably stale (written by older parse.py), so current-markup compatibility is unconfirmed.

The exact root cause and timeline of the meta.json vs bestsellers.json divergence (books/135 vs no-books/120) and the empty keywords.json — confirmed inconsistent on disk, but I could not run the scraper to reproduce which run wrote which file (a concurrent refresh is active).
Real-world ban risk of the current cadence on the user's residential IP — cannot be measured without live runs; assessed only against the spec's documented thresholds.
Behavior of run.py when a category renders 5-14 rows in practice (degraded ingest) — reasoned from code (len<5 guard) but not observed live.

dimensions.summary: The seam is well-architected: data.ts is the single import surface, all 8 read functions preserve their exact public signatures, and real-store.ts projects the scraper JSON onto the unchanged types.ts domain model. demandBand is correctly category-relative in BOTH paths (control C1 preserved), BSR correctly uses the leaf-category rank (bsr[last]), and provenance/confidence flags are honest on the real path. However, the dimension's core fear — "seed silently leaks alongside real data" — is REALIZED in two confirmed ways. (1) getKeywords falls back to fabricated SEED keywords whenever real keywords.json is empty (it currently is: keywords:[]), so the live dashboard/Demand-Radar shows REAL amazon.eg products next to SEED iphone/laptop keywords stamped with a google_trends provenance badge. (2) Non-atomic scraper writes (run.py write_text, no tmp+rename) against a 140KB file, combined with a bare try/catch in real-store that swallows JSON.parse errors and returns null, means a concurrent scrape can flip available() to false mid-request on dynamically-rendered pages, silently serving an ENTIRE seed page. Additionally getWatchlist() hardcodes three seed ASINs and resolves them with getProduct(asin)! — under real data these return undefined, producing WatchlistItem.product === undefined, which the WatchCard client component dereferences (p.bsr) and will crash. The seed-vs-real gate is all-or-nothing (zero ASIN overlap) and the spec's claim that currentBsr/riseScore/toProduct "now feed real snapshots" is false — those helpers are dead code on the real path. Verdict: conditional-go, gated on the keyword leak, the watchlist null-product crash, and atomic-write/parse-error handling.

findings.area: Seed leaks into real data (keywords)
findings.issue: getKeywords delegates to real.keywords(), which returns null when the real keyword array is empty (real-store.ts:223 `if (!kw.length) return null`). data.ts:285-286 treats null as 'no real data' and falls through to the SEED keyword synthesis. The live keywords.json currently contains `"keywords": []`, so RIGHT NOW the app emits fabricated seed keywords (iphone/laptop/etc. with synthetic demandScore and trend) on the /keywords page AND in getDashboardSummary().topKeywords — sitting next to REAL amazon.eg best-sellers. The seed branch even stamps provenance source 'amazon_autocomplete' / note 'Estimated demand', i.e. fake data wearing a real-looking provenance badge. This is the exact null-vs-seed fallback hazard: real-empty is indistinguishable from real-absent, and the user sees invented search demand presented as a live signal.
findings.evidence: real-store.ts:223 `if (!kw.length) return null;`. data.ts:285 `const realKw = real.keywords(opts); if (realKw) return realKw;` then builds from seed KEYWORDS. keywords.json verified on disk: {"scraped_at":"2026-06-08T08:27:46Z","keywords":[]}. trends worker has not populated it, so the fallback is active in production, not theoretical.
findings.impact: Users researching demand see entirely fabricated keyword demand scores mixed into an otherwise-real dashboard, with a provenance badge that implies they came from Amazon/Trends. Directly violates the platform's stated Critical control that an estimate must never be presented as ground truth, and is undetectable to the user.
findings.fix: When ANY real data is present (real.available() === true), getKeywords must NOT fall back to seed. Return an empty Keyword[] (and let the UI show an honest 'Demand signal pending — Google Trends not yet collected' empty state) instead of seed synthesis. I.e. gate the seed branch on `if (!real.available())`, mirroring the other 7 functions, rather than on whether the keyword array specifically is non-empty.

findings.area: Watchlist null-product crash under real data
findings.issue: getWatchlist() hardcodes seed ASINs ['B0EG0XIAM2','B0EG0PHIL6','B0EG0LORE9'] and builds each item as `product: getProduct(asin)!` with a non-null assertion. Under real data, getProduct delegates to real.product(asin), which searches bs.all then pr.products and returns undefined for any ASIN in neither. Verified: all three seed ASINs are absent from both real files (zero overlap between the 9 seed ASINs and the 120 real ASINs). So WatchlistItem.product is undefined at runtime; the `!` only silences the compiler. WatchCard then does `const p = item.product; ... demandBandFromBsr(p.bsr)` → reading .bsr off undefined → TypeError, crashing the /watchlists route.
findings.evidence: data.ts:355-359 maps the 3 literals to `product: getProduct(asin)!`. real-store.ts:141-157 product() returns undefined when the ASIN is in neither bs.all nor pr.products. Python check: seed∩real ASIN set = empty; B0EG0XIAM2/PHIL6/LORE9 in_real_bestsellers=False, in pr.products=False. watch-card.tsx:37 `const p = item.product;` then :41 `demandBandFromBsr(p.bsr)`.
findings.impact: The Watchlists page (a core authenticated screen) throws a runtime error and fails to render as soon as real data is live — a hard regression caused purely by the seam switch from seed to real. The non-null assertion converts a knowable undefined into a production crash.
findings.fix: getWatchlist must filter out unresolved products: `.map(asin => ({asin, addedAt, product: getProduct(asin)})).filter(x => x.product)` and type product as Product (non-optional only after the filter), OR seed the watchlist from real ASINs that actually exist (e.g. the first few of getBestSellers()). Drop the `!` assertion entirely.

findings.area: Sync fs read + non-atomic write = silent seed fallback / torn read
findings.issue: The scraper writes each JSON in place via `(OUT/'bestsellers.json').write_text(json.dumps(...))` — truncate-then-write, no temp-file + atomic rename. bestsellers.json is ~140KB. The audit context states a scrape refreshes these files concurrently. On pages that render dynamically per-request (dashboard, bestsellers, products, movers, search, keywords all `await searchParams` → dynamic), real-store does a synchronous readFileSync+JSON.parse at request time. If a request lands mid-write, JSON.parse throws on the partial file; readJson's bare `catch { return null }` swallows it, store() caches bs:null, and available() returns false → the request silently serves the ENTIRE page from SEED. There is no error, log, or 'stale data' signal — a parse failure is laundered into 'no real data → use seed'.
findings.evidence: real-store.ts:33 `} catch { return null; }` (no logging, no rethrow). available() (l.56) keys solely off `store().bs?.all?.length`, so null bs == 'fall back to seed'. run.py:98-99 `(OUT / 'bestsellers.json').write_text(json.dumps(...))` — no os.replace/tmp. mtime-cache (l.42-51) reads all three files together on any mtime change, widening the window where a half-written file is parsed.
findings.impact: During each twice-daily scrape window, dynamically-rendered requests can intermittently flip the whole UI from real to seed with no observable signal, mixing fabricated rankings/products into a 'real data' deployment. Combined with finding 1 this means seed can surface even when the operator believes the site is fully real.
findings.fix: (a) Make scraper writes atomic: write to a .tmp then os.replace() onto the final name (replace is atomic on the same filesystem). (b) In readJson, distinguish parse failure from file-absent: on a JSON.parse throw, log/surface it and prefer the last good in-memory cache rather than returning null (which is interpreted as 'no real data'). Do not let a transient parse error silently demote the whole app to seed.

findings.area: Latent category mismapping in product() fallback
findings.issue: product()'s enriched-only fallback constructs a synthetic row with `category: "electronics"` hardcoded when an ASIN exists in products.json but not in bs.all. That ASIN's real department is unknown at that point, so it would be force-labeled Electronics, giving a wrong categoryNode and (via CATEGORY_BY_NODE) a wrong categoryName, and the fallback also omits title_ar (Arabic title silently dropped). Currently latent — all 8 enriched ASINs are also in bs.all, so the branch isn't exercised — but it will misfire the moment enrichment outlives a best-seller listing (a product drops off the chart but its detail page is still cached in products.json).
findings.evidence: real-store.ts:152 `category: "electronics"` literal in the fallback object; no title_ar key passed. Verified products.json asins-not-in-bestsellers = [] today, so the path is unreached but live in code.
findings.impact: A beauty/home/fashion product that has rolled off the best-seller list would be mislabeled as Electronics on its detail page and lose its Arabic title — a real-data correctness defect that surfaces only over time, making it easy to miss in testing.
findings.fix: Derive the category from the enriched product's own leaf BSR (the bsr array's broad/department entry already names e.g. 'Beauty'/'Home & Kitchen') and map it to a node, or carry the source category on the enriched record. At minimum pass through enr's title_ar/brand and avoid a hardcoded department.

findings.area: O(n^2) seam access on list pages (per-row fs+find)
findings.issue: RankRow calls getBsrHistory(p.asin) for every row to draw a sparkline. On the real path this runs real.bsrHistory(), which does a linear `bs.all.find(asin)` (O(n)) plus three statSync calls via store() per invocation. The bestsellers page renders up to all rows (120 today), so one page does ~120 linear scans of the 120-item array (O(n^2)) and ~360 statSync syscalls. Functionally correct, but it scales poorly and re-stat's the filesystem on every row.
findings.evidence: rank-row.tsx:13 `getBsrHistory(p.asin).points...` inside a component rendered per row. real-store.ts:170 `(store().bs?.all ?? []).find((r)=>r.asin===asin)` per call; store() (l.40-51) runs statSync x3 each call (cache short-circuits the parse, not the stat). bestSellers() returns the full list (no default limit) at data.ts:177-186.
findings.impact: Wasted CPU/syscalls per request on the largest list pages; the cost grows quadratically with catalog size once category coverage expands beyond 120 items. Also the real bsrHistory returns a single point (length-1 series), so the sparkline is degenerate regardless.
findings.fix: Pass the already-loaded BsrHistory/series down from the page (which already holds the rows) instead of re-fetching per row, or memoize an asin→row index map in real-store. Given real history is length 1, consider hiding the spark until >=2 snapshots exist.

findings.area: Spec-vs-code drift: seed BSR helpers are dead on the real path (no functional bug)
findings.issue: The pipeline spec asserts currentBsr/riseScore/toProduct/demandBandForAsin are kept 'as-is — they already operate on whatever BSR series they're given; now fed real snapshots instead of synthesized ones.' In the actual code, every real-data entry point (getProduct/getBestSellers/getMovers/getReviews/getSentimentSummary/getBsrHistory/searchProducts/getKeywords) short-circuits to real-store BEFORE these helpers run, and real-store builds products/bands independently. So under real data these seed helpers are never invoked — they are NOT 'fed real snapshots'; they are inert. demandBandForAsin is exported but only self-referenced. No runtime bug, but the integration narrative misrepresents how the real path computes demand band and BSR (real uses bandFromPos over the committed list position; seed uses currentBsr percentile). Worth flagging because it means there are TWO independent demand-band implementations to keep in sync (data.ts demandBandForAsin and real-store bandFromPos) — they currently agree on thresholds (0.2/0.45/0.75) but could silently diverge.
findings.evidence: data.ts:166-167,178-179,189-190,etc. each begin `if (real.available()) return real.<fn>(...)`. real-store bandFromPos (l.66-73) duplicates the 0.2/0.45/0.75 cutoffs from data.ts demandBandForAsin (l.130-133). grep shows currentBsr/riseScore/toProduct referenced only within data.ts seed branches.
findings.impact: Maintenance hazard: the demand-band thresholds are defined in two places; a future edit to one (e.g. data.ts) would not affect the live real path, producing inconsistent bands between seed-fallback and real renders. Also the spec overstates code reuse, which can mislead reviewers into thinking the helpers are load-bearing for real data.
findings.fix: Either route real-store's band logic through the exported demandBandForAsin thresholds (single source of truth), or add a shared constant for the cutoffs imported by both. Update spec §5.4 to state the real path uses real-store.bandFromPos, not the seed helpers.

verified: All 8 public seam functions preserve their exact signatures across the seed→real switch — getBsrHistory(asin):BsrHistory, getProduct(asin,period?):Product|undefined, getBestSellers(q):RankingRow[], getMovers(q):RankingRow[], getReviews(asin,opts):Review[], getSentimentSummary(asin):SentimentSummary, getKeywords(opts):Keyword[], searchProducts(query,period?):Product[]. real-store exposes matching return types and no screen/type changes are required (data.ts:66,165,177,188,220,245,284,310).

Delegation pattern is correct for 7 of 8 functions: each does `if (real.available()) return real.<fn>(...)` then falls to seed, and real.available() is a single honest gate keyed on bs.all.length (real-store.ts:55-57).

DemandBand is category-relative in BOTH paths (control C1 preserved): seed demandBandForAsin ranks within p.categoryNode peers (data.ts:121-134); real bandFromPos ranks within the per-category list position from bs.categories (real-store.ts:66-83). Neither applies a global cross-category threshold. Verified all 120 real ASINs are present in bs.categories, so posMap resolves a band for every row (no spurious 'unknown').

BSR uses the LEAF rank, not the list/department rank: real.leafBsr returns bsr[bsr.length-1] (real-store.ts:85-88), and the real data's bsr array is ordered [department, leaf] (e.g. B0CPC8JMCW = [Electronics #1, USB Cables #1]); rowToProduct uses leaf.rank for product.bsr (l.104). Matches the spec's 'leaf rank is the meaningful key'.

Provenance/confidence is honest on the real path: facts (price/rating/reviews) carry confidence 'high', isEstimated false (real-store.ts:108-113); BSR snapshot history carries 'medium' (l.175); sentiment carries 'low' + isEstimated true with a truncated-sample note (l.211-216); fetchedAt is sourced from the real scraped_at, not a fabricated time (l.62-63).

titleAr is genuinely sourced from a separate Arabic fetch, not machine-translated: run.py:59 fetches /-/ar/gp/bestsellers/<slug> and run.py:66 joins ar_titles onto each row by ASIN; real-store maps row.title_ar straight through (l.96). The seam correctly keeps titleEn/titleAr independent (types.ts:50-51). The fact that current data shows identical EN/AR strings is a seller-localization artifact (these sellers used Latin titles on both locales), not a seam defect.

mtime cache busts correctly on data refresh: store() sums statSync mtimeMs across all three files and rebuilds the in-memory cache when the sum changes (real-store.ts:40-53); a missing file contributes 0 via catch. This correctly picks up a fresh scrape on the next request for runtime-rendered pages.

Category node mapping is consistent: all 8 real row.category strings (electronics/beauty/home/fashion/toys/grocery/baby/health) have matching CATEGORY_BY_NODE entries, so categoryName resolves for every real row (real-store.ts:99).

getMovers honestly returns [] on the real path (real-store.ts:137-139) because .eg Movers is empty and only 1 daily snapshot exists — no fabricated velocity, matching the spec's derived-movers decision. (Consumer impact noted: product page moverRow is always undefined under real data, so demand-band/gain context there defaults to 'unknown'/0 — acceptable but worth a UI empty state.)
notVerified: Whether the fs reads actually succeed in a real `next build` + `next start` on Vercel. dimensions.dimension: Calculation Engine re-audit (regression check) — web/src/lib/fees.ts + calculator-form.tsx
dimensions.summary: Re-derived the 14% VAT / referral-tier / FBA-band / break-even math by hand and against 40,000 randomized cases; the engine reproduces every documented formula with NO arithmetic, sign, or VAT regression. The VAT model is correct and subtle in the right way: consumer price is VAT-inclusive (registered revenue = price/1.14, fees.ts:130), 14% VAT is charged on Amazon's fees (fees.ts:136-137), and the registered-seller reclaim is netted via `feeVatCost = referralVat + fbaVat - reclaimableVat` (fees.ts:138-140) where reclaimableVat is the round2 of the SUM — a deliberate construction that makes the residual cost exactly 0 for registered sellers (verified 0/3000+ across all FBA rungs) and makes the on-screen line items reconcile to the headline net profit (0 mismatches / 20,000 random cases) and the cost lines reconcile to Total cost (0 / 10,000). Piecewise referral, min-fee floor, FBA ~350 price-band split, and the bisection break-even with can-never-break-even NaN guard all match the spec (01-product-spec.md:224-228). Fees are clearly and persistently disclosed as estimates (constants.ts:116 DISCLOSURE.estimatedFeesEn shown in a ConfidenceBadge=medium at the result header, in the footer with the as-of date, and as a runtime warning pushed into result.warnings at fees.ts:151-153; the products-page preview is labeled 'Est. referral fee ≈', products/[asin]/page.tsx:225). The only real spec deviations are a Grocery min-fee that should not exist and scope reductions (missing Jewelry tier; omitted storage/subscription/ads/returns inputs) — none of which produces a wrong number for an input the UI actually accepts, except the small Grocery floor.

findings.area: Referral fee — Grocery minimum (spec deviation / slight over-charge)
findings.issue: The Grocery referral rule sets `minFeeEgp: 3`, but the authoritative spec explicitly states Grocery has NO minimum referral fee (line 224: 'Grocery 4%≤250 + 10% above, no minimum'). computeReferralFee applies the floor at fees.ts:95, so any grocery item whose computed referral (4% of price) is below EGP 3 — i.e. consumer price below EGP 75 — is over-charged up to ~EGP 3 of fee, slightly understating net profit and overstating break-even for cheap grocery items.
findings.evidence: Worked case: price 50 EGP grocery → raw referral = 50×0.04 = 2.00, but engine returns max(2.00, 3) = 3.00 (reproduced). Spec line 224 says no minimum for Grocery. All other categories' min-fees (5, and Books 3) are consistent with the 'max(rate·P, 5 EGP)' spec wording; only Grocery is called out as min-exempt.
findings.impact: Bounded, small: error ≤ EGP 3 per unit and only on grocery items priced under ~75 EGP. Direction is conservative (slightly pessimistic margin), so it cannot make a losing deal look profitable. Not a VAT or sign error.
findings.fix: Set Grocery `minFeeEgp: null` in DEFAULT_FEE_SCHEDULE (fees.ts:47) to match the spec; computeReferralFee already handles null via the `!= null` guard (fees.ts:95). Then spot-confirm against sell.amazon.eg/pricing per the file's own asOf discipline.

findings.area: Coverage — Jewelry tier specced but absent
findings.issue: The spec lists Jewelry as a tiered referral category (19% ≤5,000 EGP + 5% above, 01-product-spec.md:224 / 03-feasibility-verdict.md:97), but Jewelry is absent from both the fee schedule and the user-selectable CATEGORIES list. Grep confirms zero occurrences of 'jewel' anywhere in lib/ or app/.
findings.evidence: `grep -rni jewel web/src/lib web/src/app` → NONE. The schedule has 12 categories; Jewelry is not one of them, and CATEGORY_BY_NODE has no jewelry key, so the calculator cannot model the highest-referral category Amazon EG charges.
findings.impact: No wrong number is ever shown (the category can't be selected), but a real seller researching jewelry cannot use the tool and would be silently routed to the generic 'home'/12% fallback only if some upstream code passed an unknown node. For the calculator UI specifically this is a coverage gap, not a miscalculation.
findings.fix: Add the Jewelry ReferralRule ({uptoEgp:5000, rate:0.19},{uptoEgp:null, rate:0.05}) and a corresponding CATEGORIES entry, or document the omission. Lower priority than confirming the existing rates.

findings.area: Implemented scope vs specced calculator inputs
findings.issue: Spec E1 defines the calculator inputs to include months-in-storage, monthly subscription (Pro plan), units/month, ad cost/unit, and returns % — plus EasyShip/MFN fulfilment. The implemented form supports only sell price, COGS, category, FBA/FBM, FBA size tier, inbound, misc, and the VAT toggle. Storage rate (storageEgpPerCuFtMonth:4) exists in the schedule (fees.ts:28, types.ts:180) but is never consumed by computeProfit.
findings.evidence: computeProfit (fees.ts:120-181) references vatRate, referral, fbaLadder, fbaPriceBandEgp only; `storageEgpPerCuFtMonth` is defined but has zero readers (no grep hit outside the schedule/type). The form has no storage/ads/returns fields.
findings.impact: Not a calculation error — every formula the engine DOES compute is correct. It is a completeness gap: 'misc cost' is offered as the catch-all for ad/returns/storage amortisation (hint at line 369), so users can still approximate, but a naive user may omit storage/ad drag and overstate profit. Acceptable as an MVP scope reduction if documented.
findings.fix: Either wire storage/ads/returns as first-class inputs (storage formula already has a rate to use), or explicitly state in the UI/disclosure that storage, ad spend, and returns must be folded into 'Misc cost'. The current 'misc' hint partially does this.

verified: 14% VAT model is correct end-to-end: VAT-registered net revenue = price/(1+vatRate) (fees.ts:130); 14% VAT charged on referral and FBA fees (fees.ts:136-137); reclaim netted so registered fee-VAT cost = 0, non-registered fee-VAT is a real cost (fees.ts:138-140). Matches spec lines 99/206/226 exactly.

Registered-seller fee-VAT residual is EXACTLY zero for all fee combinations: round2(refVat)+round2(fbaVat)-round2(refVat+fbaVat) tested across 0–3000 EGP referral × all 8 FBA fee values → 0 nonzero cases. The 'subtract the rounded sum' design (not sum of rounded parts) is the reason and is deliberately correct.

On-screen line items reconcile to the headline: netRevenue − referralFee − referralVat − fbaFee − fbaVat + reclaimable − COGS − inbound − misc == displayed netProfit in 0 mismatches / 20,000 randomized cases. Cost lines reconcile to 'Total cost' in 0 / 10,000 non-registered cases. No display desync.

Piecewise referral fee is correct: each tier's rate applies only to the price portion within its band; Electronics-Accessories 15%≤1000 then 8% → price 1500 yields 150+40=190 EGP (reproduced); Grocery 4%≤250 then 10% computed correctly. Min-fee floor applied after summation (fees.ts:95). Matches spec line 224 tier breakpoints.

FBA price-band split is correct: fee = high when price > 350, low otherwise (fees.ts:107). Boundary verified — exactly 350 uses the LOW fee, 350.01 uses HIGH (defensible '>' convention). FBA fee is 0 for FBM and 0 when size tier unset (fees.ts:99-108), with a warning surfaced (fees.ts:158-160).

Break-even solver is correct and robust: bisection over price with monotonic profit; expands hi up to 40× and returns NaN when a deal can never break even (fees.ts:195-196); UI renders '—' when !Number.isFinite (calculator-form.tsx:199,546). Reproduced break-even for the default preset (≈263.42 EGP, net≈0 at solution, negative one EGP below). Matches spec line 228.

Sign handling is correct for losses: negative net profit → negative margin and ROI, UI prepends '−' and switches tone/badge to 'Loss' (calculator-form.tsx:423,438,450,462). Inputs clamped non-negative via Math.max(0,…) (fees.ts:125-128) and the num() parser (calculator-form.tsx:156-159); no NaN/Infinity/divide-by-zero (margin/ROI guarded by price>0 and investment>0, fees.ts:146-148).

Estimate disclosure is persistent and not buried: DISCLOSURE.estimatedFeesEn (constants.ts:116) appears as a ConfidenceBadge confidence='medium' on the result header (calculator-form.tsx:407), in the footer with the schedule as-of date (line 588-589), AND pushed into result.warnings whenever provenance.isEstimated (fees.ts:151-153). Schedule carries provenance.isEstimated=true / confidence='medium' (fees.ts:65-71). Products-page referral preview labeled 'Est. referral fee ≈' (products/[asin]/page.tsx:225).

round2 uses Math.round((n+EPSILON)*100)/100 (fees.ts:224-226) and stays in sync with the Intl 2-dp display formatter (formatEgp, format.ts:8-22) across .005-boundary spot checks — no display/engine rounding divergence.

Fee rates are versioned not hard-coded: schedule carries asOf='2026-06-08' and an editable structure (fees.ts:24, types.ts:177), satisfying spec risk #9 (01-product-spec.md:97). The second consumer (products/[asin]/page.tsx:119-121) reuses getReferralRule/computeReferralFee consistently — no divergent re-implementation of the math.
notVerified: Absolute correctness of the fee RATES/bands themselves (8% Electronics, 12% Home, 350 EGP band, FBA EGP ladder values, etc.) against the live sell.amazon.eg/pricing page — out of scope by instruction (no fetch) and the code itself flags isEstimated=true and 'spot-confirm' (fees.ts:13,70). This audit verifies the MATH given the schedule, not the schedule's real-world accuracy.

Whether Egyptian referral fee is legally charged on the VAT-inclusive consumer price (as implemented, computeReferralFee(price,…) uses full price) vs a VAT-exclusive base — the spec itself flags 'referral on item-vs-item+shipping not isolated for EG — verify' (01-product-spec.md:229). No EG-specific source in-repo resolves this; if Amazon EG charges referral on the net-of-VAT price, every referral fee here is ~14% too high. Flagged as a documented open question, not confirmed either way.

Whether the margin denominator choice (netProfit / VAT-inclusive sellPrice, fees.ts:146, labeled 'of sell price') is the metric users expect; margin on net revenue (price/1.14) would read ~5 points higher (36.2% vs 41.3% for the default case). The label is literally accurate, so this is an interpretation note rather than an error — not independently validated against a tax/finance reference.

Runtime/browser behavior of the form (state, recompute-on-keystroke, deep-link presets) was not executed — per instructions no dev/build was run. Findings are from static derivation of the pure functions and the JSX render logic only.

VAT-reclaim treatment realism (registered sellers fully reclaiming input VAT on Amazon fees) — the spec explicitly tags this 'confirm with EG tax advisor' (01-product-spec.md:229). The engine implements full reclaim; whether that matches actual EG tax rules is outside code-correctness and unverified.

dimensions.dimension: Data Accuracy & Honesty / Disclosure (real amazon.eg data)
dimensions.summary: The platform was clearly engineered with disclosure discipline as a first-class control, and on the read-path that flows through real-store.ts most of it holds: a persistent CalibrationNotice renders on every rank/demand screen; ConfidenceBadge/ProvenanceHint label price/rating/reviews as facts and BSR/demand/sentiment/keywords as estimates; demand bands are computed within-category (audit C1) in BOTH data.ts and real-store.ts; reviews show honest N-of-M coverage; keyword demand is framed as relative interest with role=meter 0-100 and a word-only trend chip (no fabricated %); Movers correctly returns an empty list on day-1 (only one snapshot); the fee calculator is deterministic math, badged "estimated," and warns to verify. However, with REAL data now active, several places present modeled or non-existent signals as fact and one disclosure is factually false. CRITICAL: the product-detail chart is hard-titled "Rank & price history (90 days)" but real-store.bsrHistory() emits exactly ONE point (today's leaf-category BSR + today's price), so a single snapshot is dressed as a 90-day trend; and the sentiment split renders a definitive "0% positive / 100% neutral / 0% negative" bar because the scraper attaches NO sentiment field to real reviews (sentiment is only set in seed templates), actively mislabeling mostly-5-star reviews as "neutral" rather than "not analyzed." HIGH: web/src/components/app/watchlists/_components/watch-card.tsx computes the demand band from ABSOLUTE cross-category BSR cutoffs (bsr<300 => very-high), the exact misleading cross-category leaderboard the rest of the codebase forbids — and because real leaf BSR is a tiny sub-category rank, nearly everything inflates to "Very High"; the Watchlists/Alerts screens are seeded with 3 hardcoded ASINs absent from real data, so they fabricate "tracked" products (real titles never scraped) and getProduct(asin)! risks a null-deref crash in real mode; and the Settings "No personal data — reviewer names dropped at ingest" guardrail is FALSE since real reviews store and the product page renders author names (e.g., "Medhat M."). MEDIUM: keyword provenance is mislabeled "google_trends" in real-store though the real source is Amazon autocomplete (+optional Trends); real review dates show "—" because raw "Reviewed in Egypt on 3 May 2026" strings are never parsed; the Search results header "Ranked as shown on amazon.eg" overstates a title-substring filter as a real SERP ranking (contradicting its own honest caption); and the product "Rank velocity / Holding steady" KPI implies a measured velocity that cannot exist from one snapshot. Net: the disclosure scaffolding is strong, but the now-real data is shown through several seed-era surfaces that overstate history, sentiment, demand, and provenance — and one privacy disclosure is contradicted by the data on disk.

findings.area: Single snapshot shown as 90-day trend
findings.issue: The rank/price history card is hard-titled "Rank & price history (90 days)" for every product, but in real mode getBsrHistory() returns exactly ONE point: leaf-category BSR at scraped_at plus one price point. A chart explicitly labelled 90 days renders a single datapoint, implying three months of tracked history that does not exist.
findings.evidence: page.tsx:281 literal `Rank & price history (90 days)`. real-store.ts:171-174 `points: leaf ? [{ date, value: leaf.rank }] : []`, `pricePoints: row?.price_egp != null ? [{ date, value: row.price_egp }] : []`. products.json bsr array is category bands ([{rank,category:Electronics},{rank,category:USB Cables}]) not a time series; leafBsr() takes b[b.length-1] (one value).
findings.impact: A user reads a 90-day rank/price trend into one snapshot — the core 'single BSR snapshot shown as a 90-day trend' failure mode. Undermines every downside/sourcing decision built on perceived history.
findings.fix: Make the title dynamic from the actual span: when points.length<2 render 'Rank & price history (tracking just started — 1 snapshot)' and show a single dot/empty-state instead of '(90 days)'. Drive the label off history.points length/date-range, not a constant.

findings.area: Unclassified sentiment presented as computed 'neutral'
findings.issue: Real reviews carry no sentiment field (parse.py never classifies; sentiment is only attached to seed REVIEW_TEMPLATES). real-store.sentimentSummary() therefore computes pos=0,neg=0 => positivePct=0, neutralPct=100, negativePct=0, and the product page draws a confident stacked 'Sentiment split' bar reading 100% Neutral / 0% Positive / 0% Negative.
findings.evidence: parse.py reviews_list fields = [author,body,date,helpful,lang,rating,review_id,title,verified] — no sentiment. real-store.ts:199-207 `pos = rl.filter(r=>r.sentiment==='positive')...` always 0. Reproduced on B0CPC8JMCW: 8 reviews rated [5,4,5,5,5,4,5,1] render as positivePct=0/neutralPct=100/negativePct=0.
findings.impact: Overwhelmingly positive reviews are misrepresented to the user as 'neutral'. 'Not analyzed' is shown as a definitive sentiment result — a direct data-honesty violation despite the 'low' badge.
findings.fix: When no review carries a sentiment label, do NOT emit a 0/100/0 split. Either classify (even rating-derived: >=4 positive, ==3 neutral, <=2 negative, labelled 'derived from star rating'), or render an explicit 'Sentiment not analyzed for this item' empty-state and suppress the split bar.

findings.area: Cross-category absolute BSR demand band (audit C1 violation)
findings.issue: WatchCard derives the demand band from ABSOLUTE BSR thresholds (bsr<300 very-high, <1000 high, <3000 moderate, else low) applied across all categories — the exact misleading cross-category leaderboard the codebase forbids elsewhere (data.ts:120-122 and real-store.ts:66 both compute band by WITHIN-category percentile). The comment even claims it 'Mirrors the thresholds in @/lib/data#demandBandFor', which is false.
findings.evidence: watch-card.tsx:27-31 `if (bsr<300) 'very-high'; if (bsr<1000)'high'...`. demandBandForAsin (data.ts:121-134) and bandFromPos (real-store.ts:67-73) instead use idx/(n-1) within categoryNode. In real mode product.bsr is the leaf-category rank (USB Cables #1), so almost every watched item collapses to 'Very High'.
findings.impact: The same product shows a different, inflated demand band on the Watchlist than on Best Sellers/Products/detail — and leaf-rank inflation manufactures false 'Very High' demand, the precise dishonesty the rest of the app engineers against.
findings.fix: Delete demandBandFromBsr; pass the within-category band through the WatchlistItem (compute via demandBandForAsin / bandFromPos) so the band matches every other surface and stays category-relative.

findings.area: Fabricated 'tracked' items + null-deref in real mode
findings.issue: getWatchlist() (and getAlerts()) hardcode seed ASINs B0EG0XIAM2/B0EG0PHIL6/B0EG0LORE9 that do not exist in the real dataset, and map them with getProduct(asin)! (non-null assertion). In real mode real.product() returns undefined for these ASINs, so WatchCard receives product:undefined and reads p.titleEn -> runtime crash; Alerts shows seed titles ('Redmi Buds 5','Philips Airfryer') that were never scraped.
findings.evidence: data.ts:355 `['B0EG0XIAM2','B0EG0PHIL6','B0EG0LORE9'].map(asin=>({...product:getProduct(asin)!}))`. Verified none of the 3 ASINs are among the 120 real ASINs in bestsellers.json/products.json. getProduct->real.product (real-store.ts:141-157) returns undefined when ASIN absent.
findings.impact: Either a crashed Watchlists page or a watchlist/alerts list of fabricated products presented as real tracked Egypt items — misleading and broken under real data.
findings.fix: Source watchlist/alerts seed ASINs from the live dataset (e.g. first N of getBestSellers()), drop the non-null assertion, and filter out any item whose product is undefined.

findings.area: False privacy/compliance disclosure vs data on disk
findings.issue: Settings states as a guardrail: 'Reviewer names and any personal information are dropped at ingest; only aggregate signals are kept.' This is false: the scraper captures author names, real-store maps authorName=r.author, and the product page renders {review.authorName} for each review.
findings.evidence: products.json review has `author: "Medhat M."`. parse.py:156 `"author": au.get_text(...)`. real-store.ts:188 `authorName: r.author`. page.tsx:530 `{review.authorName}`.
findings.impact: A stated privacy/ethics commitment is contradicted by the live build — the most serious kind of honesty defect for an institutional/compliance review; it also stores PII the policy claims it discards.
findings.fix: Either actually drop author names at ingest (parse.py) and stop rendering authorName, or correct the Settings copy to state that public reviewer display names are retained and shown. Make the claim and the data match.

findings.area: Keyword provenance label mismatch
findings.issue: real-store keywords() stamps provenance source 'google_trends' with note 'Google Trends Egypt — relative interest', but the real keyword source is Amazon EG search autocomplete (completion.amazon.co.uk), with Google Trends only an optional best-effort 'rising' tag. Conversely the dashboard/keywords UI says purely 'Amazon search autocomplete'. Neither label matches the actual hybrid source.
findings.evidence: trends.py module docstring 'PRIMARY source: Amazon EG search autocomplete... OPTIONAL: Google Trends EG to tag rising terms'; output source string line 102 = 'amazon_eg_autocomplete (completion.amazon.co.uk) + google_trends'. real-store.ts:232 hardcodes source 'google_trends'. keywords.json currently keywords:[] (empty), so the seed-autocomplete path is what actually renders today.
findings.impact: Provenance shown to the user is wrong about where demand came from; an auditor cannot reconcile the displayed source with the pipeline. Lower severity because it is source attribution, not a value, but provenance honesty is a stated control.
findings.fix: Set the keyword provenance source to the true value (amazon_eg_autocomplete with optional trends-rising), and align the dashboard/keywords copy to 'Amazon autocomplete (+ Google Trends rising tags)'.

findings.area: Real review dates render as em-dash
findings.issue: Real review date is the raw string 'Reviewed in Egypt on 3 May 2026'; real-store passes it straight to reviewedAt, and formatDate does new Date(str) -> NaN -> returns '—'. Every real review shows date '—'.
findings.evidence: parse.py:158 `"date": dt.get_text(strip=True)` => 'Reviewed in Egypt on 3 May 2026'. real-store.ts:189 `reviewedAt: r.date`. format.ts:65-66 NaN guard returns '—'.
findings.impact: Not a false claim, but every real review loses its date, degrading trust and making recency impossible to judge. A reviewer could mistake '—' for missing data rather than a parse failure.
findings.fix: Parse the 'Reviewed in Egypt on <date>' pattern to ISO in parse.py (or real-store), then pass a real ISO date; fall back to omitting the date row when unparseable rather than showing '—'.

findings.area: Substring filter overstated as live SERP ranking
findings.issue: The results header says 'Ranked as shown on amazon.eg', but real.search() merely filters the cached best-seller 'all' array by case-insensitive title substring — there is no live SERP query and no Amazon search ranking. This directly contradicts the page's own honest caption that says results are 'not a live ranked index'.
findings.evidence: search/page.tsx:143 `Ranked as shown on {MARKETPLACE.domain}`. real-store.ts:162-164 filters store().bs.all by title.includes(q). SerpProvenanceCaption (page.tsx:40-44) correctly says 'not a live ranked index'.

dimensions.summary: Audited the launchd scheduling, single-instance lock, logging, kill-switch propagation, laptop-sleep failure mode, the Option-A "cron commits data → Vercel" flow, and the DEPLOY.md runbook against the real files in /Users/home/Documents/Amazon. The local scrape mechanics are mostly sound: the agent is loaded in launchctl, the lock uses atomic mkdir with an EXIT trap, the in-process Blocked kill-switch stops a run cleanly, run duration (~6 min) fits comfortably inside the 12h gap, and the read-side (real-store.ts) degrades gracefully on missing/corrupt JSON. HOWEVER the headline deploy story does NOT hold as written. The Option-A pipeline is non-functional today: the git push line that DEPLOY.md tells you to "append" to run_daily.sh is ABSENT from the script, the repo has ZERO commits (no HEAD), NO git remote, and web/src/data/real/*.json is entirely UNTRACKED — so nothing is committed, nothing pushes, and a Vercel build would see no data. Compounding ops gaps: the pmset wake covers only the 09:05 morning slot while the plist also fires at 21:13 (every evening run is silently lost when the lid is closed); there is no failure alerting at all (a block or empty scrape is silent); JSON writes are non-atomic (truncated-file window overlaps the mtime-cache reader); launchd StdOut/Err logs grow unbounded with no rotation; and the unattended git PAT/credential is hand-waved. Net: solid local data-collection harness, but the "live site shows fresh Egypt data" claim is Not Verified and currently false end-to-end.

findings.area: Deploy / Option-A pipeline integrity
findings.issue: The Option-A 'cron commits data then Vercel redeploys' flow is documented but NOT implemented. DEPLOY.md tells the operator to 'append' a `git add/commit/push` line to run_daily.sh, but that line is absent from the actual script — `grep -n git scrapers/run_daily.sh` returns nothing. The scrape writes JSON and stops; nothing is ever committed or pushed.
findings.evidence: run_daily.sh ends at line 27 with `echo "=== ... done ==="`; no git invocation anywhere. `grep git scrapers/run_daily.sh` → 'NO git references'. DEPLOY.md:31-34 presents the push as a manual append the user must do.
findings.impact: The core value claim ('every scrape commits real data, Vercel rebuilds, the live site shows fresh Egypt data', DEPLOY.md:37) is false out of the box. Fresh data never leaves the laptop. Silent: the scrape 'succeeds' locally while the live site is frozen at deploy-time data forever.
findings.fix: Append the documented git step to run_daily.sh, gated on a successful scrape (rc_scrape==0 and non-empty meta.json), with explicit error logging. Better: make it part of the committed script, not a manual edit, so the runbook and reality cannot drift.

findings.area: Deploy / git repository state
findings.location: repo root (git rev-parse HEAD, git ls-files, git remote -v)
findings.issue: The repository is not deploy-ready at all: it has ZERO commits (no HEAD), NO configured remote, and NOTHING tracked — `git ls-files | wc -l` = 0. Every path (scrapers/, web/, DEPLOY.md, data) shows as untracked '??' in git status. web/src/data/real/*.json is therefore not under version control.
findings.evidence: `git rev-parse HEAD` → 'fatal: ... unknown revision' (NO COMMITS YET). `git remote -v` → empty. `git ls-files` → 0 files. `git status --porcelain` shows only '??' entries. The four JSON data files exist on disk (bestsellers/products/meta/keywords.json) but `git ls-files web/src/data` is empty.
findings.impact: Even if the push line existed, there is no remote to push to and no committed baseline, so `git push` would fail. Vercel (which builds from a git push) would have no repo and no data files. The entire Option-A path is blocked at step 0. DEPLOY.md:79-80 lists 'Push repo to GitHub' as a checkbox but the runbook never states the repo is currently uninitialized for remote.
findings.fix: Document and perform the real bootstrap: git init state, create the GitHub remote (the github integration is connected), commit a baseline INCLUDING web/src/data/real, add the remote, push once. Confirm web/src/data/real is intended to be committed (not gitignored) — currently there is no .gitignore at all, which is its own risk (logs, .env.local, node_modules could get committed).

findings.area: Scheduling / laptop-sleep failure mode
findings.issue: The pmset wake schedule does not cover the evening run. plist fires at 09:07 AND 21:13, but the runbook only sets `pmset repeat wakeorpoweron MTWRFSU 09:05:00` — a single morning wake. Every 21:13 run is silently missed whenever the machine is asleep at night (the common case for a laptop).
findings.evidence: plist StartCalendarInterval: Hour 9/Minute 7 and Hour 21/Minute 13. DEPLOY.md:18 and :77 both specify only 09:05:00 in the pmset command. `pmset repeat` supports only one wake time; there is no second entry for ~21:11.
findings.impact: Half the intended twice-daily refresh never happens on a sleeping laptop → at best once-daily data, at worst stale for full days. The '$0, works today' framing overstates reliability. launchd coalesces a missed StartCalendarInterval to run once on next wake, so the morning run may catch up — but a machine that is fully shut down at fire time loses the run entirely with no catch-up.
findings.fix: Either schedule both wakes (`pmset repeat wakeorpoweron MTWRFSU 09:05:00 wakeorpoweron MTWRFSU 21:11:00` — note pmset's two-event syntax) or document caffeinate/keep-plugged for both windows. Also widen the morning lead time: 09:05 wake → 09:07 job leaves only ~2 min for Wi-Fi reassociation; a cold wake may not have network ready, failing the first fetch.

findings.area: Observability / failure alerting
findings.location: scrapers/run_daily.sh, run.py, trends.py, fetch.py (no alerting anywhere)
findings.issue: There is no failure notification of any kind. A hard block (Blocked kill-switch), an empty/under-filled scrape, a non-residential-IP 503 storm, or a crashed run is only discoverable by manually reading log files. No mail, osascript notification, webhook, or non-zero-exit signal that anything watches.
findings.evidence: grep for mail|notify|osascript|slack|webhook|alert|sentry across all scraper files → none. run.py prints '[BLOCKED]'/'[WARN]' to stdout (→ log file) but nothing escalates. run_daily.sh captures rc_scrape (line 24) but never uses it to set the script's exit code, so even launchd sees success.
findings.impact: Operationally blind. The scraper can silently produce zero or stale data for days (e.g. IP starts getting 503, or amazon.eg markup changes and parse.parse_bestsellers returns <5 rows so every category is skipped) and the operator only finds out by chance or via the UI looking stale. For a data product this is a meaningful trust/SLA gap.
findings.fix: On block/empty-result, emit a desktop notification (osascript) and/or write a sentinel; propagate a non-zero exit from run_daily.sh when rc_scrape!=0 or meta.json product_count==0 so launchd logs and any future monitor can react. Add a simple 'last successful scrape age' check surfaced in the runbook.

findings.area: Data integrity / non-atomic writes vs live cache
findings.issue: JSON files are written non-atomically with Path.write_text (truncate-then-write). The app's real-store.ts busts its cache on file mtime and re-reads on any change, so a `npm run dev` server (or a Vercel ISR/runtime read) can read a half-written bestsellers.json during the scrape's write window. The read path catches JSON parse errors and returns null (good — degrades to seed), but the result is a transient flip of live data to seed/fallback mid-scrape rather than a clean swap.
findings.evidence: run.py uses `(OUT/'bestsellers.json').write_text(json.dumps(...))` — no temp-file + os.replace, no fsync. real-store.ts:44 sums statSync mtimeMs across the three files and re-reads (line 50) whenever the sum changes; readJson (line 28-36) try/catches and returns null on malformed JSON.
findings.impact: Concurrency-correctness defect. During each ~6-min run a reader can momentarily see truncated files (whole categories vanish to fallback) or a mixed state (new bestsellers.json + old products.json) because the three files are written sequentially, not as a set. With the prompt's own note that 'a scrape is refreshing data files concurrently', this window is live right now.
findings.fix: Write to `*.json.tmp` then `os.replace()` (atomic on same filesystem) for each file, and write all three before any swap (or write to a new timestamped dir and atomically repoint). This guarantees readers always see a complete, internally consistent snapshot.

findings.area: Kill-switch durability across runs
findings.issue: The 'stop-on-block' kill-switch is purely in-process: Blocked is raised and the current run breaks out, but nothing is persisted. The next launchd invocation (09:07/21:13, or a coalesced wake) starts completely fresh and will re-hit a still-blocking amazon.eg from the same IP — there is no cooldown/backoff that survives process exit.
findings.evidence: fetch.py has zero filesystem/env persistence (grep for open/Path/write/getenv → none outside docstring). _is_blocked returns on 403/429/503 or CAPTCHA markers; the caller just `break`s. No 'blocked_until' timestamp file is written or checked at run start.
findings.impact: The guardrail 'never retry-hammer' (fetch.py:47, DEPLOY.md:72) holds WITHIN a run but not ACROSS runs. If the IP gets soft-banned, the agent keeps probing twice a day indefinitely, which is exactly the escalation pattern the guardrails aim to avoid. Low legal-risk given polite cadence, but it undermines the stated 'low-risk lane' discipline.
findings.fix: On Blocked, write a `blocked_until` sentinel (e.g. now+24-48h) into scrapers/logs or /tmp; have run.py/run_daily.sh check it at start and exit early (logging 'in cooldown') until it expires. This makes the kill-switch durable, matching the runbook's claimed behavior.

findings.area: Logging / unbounded growth
findings.issue: No log rotation or pruning exists. run_daily.sh creates one dated file per day (scrape-YYYYMMDD.log) → unbounded file COUNT (365/yr) that is never deleted. The plist's StandardOutPath/StandardErrorPath (launchd.out.log / launchd.err.log) are SINGLE files appended on every launch forever → unbounded SIZE growth.
findings.evidence: run_daily.sh:11 `LOG=.../scrape-$(date +%Y%m%d).log`. plist:22 launchd.out.log, :24 launchd.err.log (fixed paths). grep for logrotate|truncate|find -mtime|rm log across scrapers/ + DEPLOY.md → none. (logs/ dir currently empty — agent loaded but hasn't fired yet, so growth not yet observed.)
findings.impact: Slow-burn disk/inode bloat on a personal laptop; the single launchd.*.log files in particular grow without bound and are the ones that capture stderr stack traces. Not urgent at current volume but there is no runbook step to manage it.
findings.fix: Add a prune step (e.g. `find "$LOG_DIR" -name 'scrape-*.log' -mtime +30 -delete`) in run_daily.sh and either rotate or periodically truncate launchd.out/err.log. Document log location + retention in DEPLOY.md.

findings.area: Deploy / unattended git auth
findings.issue: The unattended git push depends on a credential the runbook only mentions parenthetically ('Configure a git credential/PAT once so the unattended push works') with no concrete steps, no scope guidance, and no note on token expiry/rotation. There is also no committed remote, so the auth mechanism (HTTPS PAT in keychain/credential helper vs SSH deploy key) is unspecified.
findings.evidence: DEPLOY.md:35 single parenthetical; checklist item :80 '+ a git credential' with no procedure. No .git/config remote present (git remote -v empty), so no helper is configured.
findings.impact: The flow that is supposed to be the unattended backbone hinges on an under-specified, manually-configured secret. If the PAT expires or the credential helper isn't set for the launchd user context (launchd agents run with a minimal environment), the push fails silently (compounded by the no-alerting finding). PATs in plaintext are also a secret-management risk if mis-stored.
findings.fix: Spell out the exact one-time setup: create a fine-grained PAT (repo contents write only), store via `git credential-osxkeychain`, verify a manual `git push` works from the same shell context launchd uses, and note expiry/rotation. Confirm the credential is reachable in launchd's environment (it does not inherit your interactive shell).

findings.area: launchd robustness / log-path parent dir
findings.issue: launchd writes StandardOutPath/StandardErrorPath itself before the script runs and does NOT create missing parent directories. The script's `mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"` (run_daily.sh:10) only protects its own dated $LOG, not launchd's StdOut/Err. If scrapers/logs/ is ever deleted, launchd fails to open its log paths and the job can fail to start cleanly with no captured error.
findings.evidence: plist:22-24 fixed paths under .../scrapers/logs/. run_daily.sh mkdir runs inside the script, i.e. AFTER launchd has already tried to open StdOut/Err. logs/ currently exists so not triggered today.
findings.impact: Edge-case fragility: a cleanup that removes the logs dir silently breaks scheduling until the dir is recreated. Minor, but it is an unguarded assumption.
findings.fix: Keep a committed .gitkeep in scrapers/logs/ so the dir always exists after checkout, and note in the runbook that this directory must not be deleted (or have an install step recreate it).

findings.area: Runbook clarity / timezone assumption
findings.issue: DEPLOY.md states the agent 'runs 09:07 + 21:13 Cairo', but the plist has no TimeZoneName key, so launchd uses the machine's LOCAL timezone, not a pinned Cairo. It happens to be correct now (system TZ = Africa/Cairo), but the 'Cairo' guarantee is implicit on machine config, not on the schedule.
findings.evidence: plist StartCalendarInterval has Hour/Minute only, no TimeZoneName. `/etc/localtime -> .../Africa/Cairo` and `date` → EEST confirm it currently matches. DEPLOY.md:12 asserts 'Cairo' as if guaranteed.
findings.impact: If the laptop travels or TZ changes, the scrape silently shifts off the intended Egypt-evening/morning windows (which matter for amazon.eg traffic patterns and freshness expectations). Documentation overstates the guarantee.
findings.fix: Either add a note that times follow system TZ (and assume the box stays on Africa/Cairo) or, for a hard guarantee, document that the intent is Cairo-local and verify system TZ as an activation checklist item.

dimensions.summary: Strict audit of the Rasid amazon.eg platform for security and production readiness, evidence-based on real files under /Users/home/Documents/Amazon (no modifications, no build/fetch run). SECRETS: clean — a full-repo high-signal scan (AWS/Stripe/GitHub/Supabase JWT/PEM/firecrawl patterns) found NO committed secrets, keys, or tokens; web/.env.example contains only empty placeholders; no .env/.env.local/.env.production exists on disk; .gitignore ignores .env*. The app makes zero external network calls at runtime (all data via fs), there is no eval/Function and the single dangerouslySetInnerHTML (ui/chart.tsx) injects only developer-controlled CSS color vars, not scraped data — so no meaningful XSS sink. HOWEVER, production readiness is NOT met. The headline issue (the prompt's central question) is CONFIRMED: an fs read of web/src/data/real does NOT reliably survive a production Vercel build. The dynamic SSR routes (/, /bestsellers, /products, /movers, /keywords, /search, /products/[asin]) read the JSON at request time via path.join(process.cwd(),'src/data/real') with a runtime filename variable; @vercel/nft cannot statically trace dynamically-constructed fs paths (confirmed: the build trace .next/.../page.js.nft.json contains ZERO data/real references; grep of .next/server for data/real = 0 hits; outputFileTracingIncludes is NOT set; output is not 'standalone'). On Vercel those files will be absent from the Lambda filesystem, existsSync→false, available()→false, and the app SILENTLY falls back to fake seed data with no error surfaced. Separately, three routes (/watchlists, /alerts, /settings) are statically prerendered at BUILD time (they emit .html); /watchlists and /alerts read getProduct→fs at build, so they freeze whatever data existed at build and never refresh. There are ZERO route boundaries (no error.tsx, not-found.tsx, loading.tsx, or global-error.tsx authored — only Next's defaults), so a torn/partial JSON read throws and bubbles to a blank framework error page. The scraper writes 3 files non-atomically (Path.write_text) while the SSR app reads them concurrently — a real torn-read/JSON.parse-failure race (already visibly inconsistent on disk: meta.json product_count=135 / categories incl. 'books' vs bestsellers.json all=120). DEPLOY.md's RECOMMENDED 'commit data' path is unwired: the git push line is only described as a manual TODO, it is NOT in run_daily.sh, and the repo currently has ZERO commits, so nothing is committed/tracked yet. keywords.json is empty ({"keywords":[]}), so the live trends source is silently failing and the dashboard already serves synthetic keywords. The residential single-IP egress is a documented single point of failure; ToS posture (scraping vs Amazon CoU) is honestly acknowledged in docs as a 'tolerated breach, not permitted'. The launchd plist and run_daily.sh hardcode /Users/home/... and the spec doc commits the operator's real residential IP and ASN.

findings.area: SSR / Vercel deploy — fs read of bundled data
findings.location: web/src/lib/real-store.ts:25-36 (DIR=path.join(process.cwd(),'src/data/real'); readJson(name) with runtime filename); web/next.config.ts (no outputFileTracingIncludes); .next/server/app/(app)/page.js.nft.json (trace)
findings.issue: On a production Vercel build, the dynamic SSR routes will not have web/src/data/real/*.json in the serverless function filesystem, so the app silently serves FAKE seed data instead of real amazon.eg data.
findings.evidence: Next's own bundled docs (web/node_modules/next/dist/docs/.../output.md) state @vercel/nft 'statically analyzes import, require, and fs usage' and 'might fail to include required files' (fix = outputFileTracingIncludes). real-store builds the path with process.cwd() + a runtime-variable filename, which nft cannot statically resolve. Verified: dashboard nft trace has 'data/real hits: NONE'; `grep -r data/real web/.next/server | wc -l` = 0; outputFileTracingIncludes NONE; required-server-files.json output:None (not standalone). data.ts gates ONLY on real.available() (existsSync) with no env flag and no error — readJson swallows errors and returns null → seed fallback (data.ts:67,166,178,189,221,246,311).
findings.impact: Production site appears to work but shows fabricated seed numbers (prices/ranks/reviews) under real-data provenance labels — a silent correctness/trust failure on the platform's core value prop.
findings.fix: Do not read app-local files via process.cwd() on Vercel. Either (a) add outputFileTracingIncludes:{ '/**':['./src/data/real/**'] } (or per-route globs) in next.config.ts AND verify the trace now lists the JSON, or (b) import the JSON statically (import data from '@/data/real/bestsellers.json') so it is bundled by webpack/turbopack, or (c) move reads to Supabase (DEPLOY Option B). Then prove it: build and confirm the .nft.json for each dynamic route lists data/real, or that the JSON is in the function bundle.

findings.area: Deploy wiring — committed-data pipeline not implemented
findings.location: DEPLOY.md:24-37 (Option A 'RECOMMENDED'); scrapers/run_daily.sh:1-28 (no git step); repo git state (0 commits)
findings.issue: The recommended production deploy path (cron commits fresh data → Vercel rebuilds) is not actually wired, and the repo has never been committed, so there is no data to deploy and no mechanism to refresh it.
findings.evidence: `grep git scrapers/run_daily.sh` → none; DEPLOY.md:32-35 only tells the user to 'append' the git add/commit/push line manually. `git log` → 'your current branch main does not have any commits yet'. `git ls-files` → 0 tracked files. The data JSON is present on disk but untracked.
